name: Pantheon (MIT Media Lab) Historical Popularity Index
what: Ranking of 11,341 Wikipedia biographies present in more than 25 language editions, with verified birth date, birthplace, gender and a 3-level occupation taxonomy. Two popularity measures: L (number of language editions) and HPI, which combines L, time since birth and 2008-2013 pageviews.
why_it_matters: The closest existing people-ranking method with a published dataset and a stated formula family. It is our baseline to beat on bias; no validated alternative was found that beats it.
numbers: 11,341 biographies (MIT page, Jan 2016). HPI formula weights not published on the page. Earlier 2014 coverage cites a 15-edition threshold (sopitas.com) but the 2016 page says more than 25; treat as unresolved. Source: https://www.media.mit.edu/publications/pantheon-10-a-manually-verified-dataset-of-globally-famous-biographies/
ui_notes: Show L and HPI as separate columns with the component breakdown (languages, age, pageviews); show top-N per occupation and per country rather than one global list.
note: Biases: authors state English, Western, male and highly-educated editor bias plus recency bias; HPI uses pageviews so it skews to US and recent figures (Wikimedia Research Newsletter 2014). Pantheon 2.0 not found in search. | check: MIT Media Lab page: 11,341 biographies present in more than 25 language editions; published 5 Jan 2016. Matches.

name: Pantheon 1.0: a manually verified dataset of globally famous biographies (Yu, Ronen, Hu, Lu, Hidalgo)
what: Data paper behind Pantheon: the L and HPI measures, the occupation taxonomy, and a comparison with Murray's Human Accomplishments and with external accomplishment measures in tennis, swimming, car racing and chess.
why_it_matters: Only peer-style validation we found for a people-popularity index: popularity (L, HPI) correlates with individual accomplishment, read as a proxy for historical impact.
numbers: 11,341 biographies; more than 25 languages; pageviews 2008-2013. Correlation coefficients not shown on the MIT summary page; check the full paper. Source: https://www.media.mit.edu/publications/pantheon-10-a-manually-verified-dataset-of-globally-famous-biographies/
ui_notes: Cite the paper on the leaderboard footer; show the external-validation domains (tennis, chess) as a sanity panel.
note: Authors' own limitations: Wikipedia editors skew English, Western, male, educated, and recency-biased; the dataset is a view of multilingual Wikipedia as of May 2013.

name: Interactions of cultures and top people of Wikipedia from ranking of 24 language editions (Eom et al., PLoS ONE 2015)
what: Runs PageRank and 2DRank on the hyperlink graphs of 24 Wikipedia language editions and lists the top 100 historical figures per edition and per algorithm.
why_it_matters: A link-structure ranking of people that needs no pageview data; gives a per-language view that can be compared to pageview-based scores.
numbers: 24 language editions; top 100 per edition. Linnaeus ranks first under PageRank, Hitler first under 2DRank (Shortlist, https://shortlist.com/news/revealed-the-most-influential-people-ever). PLoS ONE 10(3): e0114825 (2015).
ui_notes: Show a per-edition toggle; show PageRank and 2DRank side by side because they disagree (Linnaeus vs. Hitler).
note: Biases: link structure rewards taxonomy and list articles (Linnaeus effect); 2DRank rewards outgoing-link density; per-language results differ sharply, so no single global order.

name: Who's Bigger? Where Historical Figures Really Rank (Skiena and Ward, 2013)
what: Book applying a PageRank-style score to the Wikipedia link graph to rank everyone with an article, with an explicit definition of significance as the social and cultural effect of an individual's achievement.
why_it_matters: The clearest public description of PageRank applied to people, and a good template for an explained composite; the reviews show how readers react to the output.
numbers: Top ranks reported in reviews: Jesus #1, Napoleon, Mohammed, Shakespeare in the top 4 (Big Think, https://develop.bigthink.com/?p=57344); Marie Antoinette 125th (SIAM News review as cited in search). Lowest-ranked example about #843,790 (review).
ui_notes: Show rank with the percentile and the rank of the same person under a second measure to expose disagreement.
note: Biases: link graph favours Western, English-heavy and historically canonical figures; reviewers question whether PageRank measures significance at all.

name: Cultural Anthropology through the Lens of Wikipedia: Historical Leader Networks, Gender Bias, and News-based Sentiment (arXiv 1508.00055)
what: Builds networks of historical leaders from Wikipedia and measures gender bias and news-based sentiment; uses Pantheon-style lists.
why_it_matters: Shows that a top-N built on Pantheon-type lists is dominated by Greek philosophers (top five: Aristotle, Plato, Jesus, Socrates, Alexander), which is the selection-bias evidence we need for our own cohort design.
numbers: Pantheon-derived list from 11,340 Wikipedia people pages; minimum 25 language editions; top five entries Aristotle, Plato, Jesus, Socrates, Alexander (per paper summary in search; verify in PDF).
ui_notes: Use as a warning panel: show how many of the top-N are from one region or era.
note: Biases: Murray Human Accomplishments source is textbook-based; leader networks inherit textbook canon.

name: Survival of the Notable: Gender Asymmetry in Wikipedia Collective Deliberations (Huq and Ciampaglia, arXiv 2411.04340; ACM HCI 2025)
what: Competing-risk survival analysis of Articles for Deletion discussions; tests how notability decisions differ for biographies of women versus men.
why_it_matters: Direct evidence that notability gatekeeping is gendered, so a ranking built on Wikipedia article existence inherits the gap before any scoring starts.
numbers: Women's biographies nominated for deletion sooner, but consensus takes longer; women's biographies more often merged into men's for historical figures (abstract, arXiv 2411.04340). Share of women biographies: 18.51% on English Wikipedia per the paper's citation of the Wikidata Human Gender Indicator.
ui_notes: Show gender share of the cohort next to every ranked list, with the cohort's expected share.
note: Bias: gender (article-level gatekeeping). Wikipedia's own page cites that 41% of AfD nominated biographies in April 2017 were about women when women were about 17% of biographies.

name: Women in Wikipedia are slightly more notable than men; gap larger for local heroes (EPJ Data Science)
what: Study of notability among biographies of women and men; finds the gender gap is larger for less-notable local figures than for superstars.
why_it_matters: A threshold-based notability cut (e.g. article exists) will admit men at lower notability and exclude women, so any rank with an existence filter needs a gender-stratified check.
numbers: Gap larger for local heroes than superstars (search summary of EPJ Data Science 2016 paper; check exact numbers in PDF).
ui_notes: Show a stratified view: rank within notability band so low-notability women are not hidden.
note: Bias: gender; glass-ceiling in inclusion barrier per authors.

name: We Need a Woman in Music: Exploring Wikipedia's Values on Article Priority (arXiv 2208.08426)
what: Studies which Wikipedia articles get priority (pageviews, editing); reports on biography gender in the top of the pageview ranking.
why_it_matters: Pageview-based fame ranks inherit editor priority; shows the bias is measurable in top-N lists.
numbers: 32% of biographies in the top 50,000 by pageviews are women; strong recency effect at the very top (search summary; verify in paper).
ui_notes: Show the gender share of the top-N against the cohort baseline on the page.
note: Bias: gender and recency; pageviews reward people in the news that year.

name: Global Gender Differences in Wikipedia Readership (Johnson et al., ICWSM)
what: Joins a global survey of 65,031 Wikipedia readers to reading logs; shows readership gender differences.
why_it_matters: Popularity rankings built on readership amplify existing imbalances unless they correct for reader gender; this is the evidence to cite for that claim.
numbers: 65,031 survey respondents plus reading logs (ICWSM abstract).
ui_notes: Caveat on pageview-based panels: say popularity reflects who reads, not only who matters.
note: Bias: gender of readers; popularity-based rankings can exacerbate imbalance.

name: QRank (Wikidata entity pageview score)
what: Weekly-published gzipped CSV ranking every Wikidata item by aggregated pageviews across Wikipedia and sister projects (Wikispecies, Wikibooks, Wikiquote and others).
why_it_matters: Joins to our people-graph by Wikidata ID; the cheapest current-popularity input we can actually get.
numbers: Score = aggregated pageviews across Wikimedia projects, no normalization described (Simon Willison, Apr 2024). Mirror SQLite DB 307MB (hikeratlas/qrank via same page).
ui_notes: Show the raw QRank and a log-scaled value; never show the raw view count as rank.
note: Biases: recency, English and US traffic, and bots/news spikes; no per-language split in the public file. | check: simonwillison.net 2024/Apr/21: QRank aggregates pageviews across Wikipedia, Wikispecies, Wikibooks, Wikiquote; gzipped CSV; mirror weekly; mirror SQLite DB 307MB. Matches.

name: Wikidata sitelink count as notability proxy
what: Count of Wikipedia language editions with an article for a Wikidata item (sitelinks). Long the default way to order Wikidata results.
why_it_matters: Cheap, cross-language breadth signal for all 339k people; available from the Wikidata dump with no pageview pipeline.
numbers: Sitelinks measure breadth across editions, not depth; the Phabricator discussion calls it not very accurate when a topic is mostly in one language (Wikimedia Phabricator; URL is a discussion task surfaced by search, content to verify).
ui_notes: Show as 'present in N editions'; use it as an input, not the headline score.
note: Bias: Western and English-heavy editions decide breadth; large-language-edition bias; sitelinks grow with age.

name: Semantic Scholar influential citations and h-index FAQ
what: Influential-citation flag from a machine-learning model using citation counts and citation context; h-index computed only from discoverable papers; the site advises against comparative use of h-index.
why_it_matters: A scholar-side impact input that already down-weights passing citations; usable for the works side of our ranking.
numbers: No single numeric threshold published in the FAQ text; flagging depends on full-text access (FAQ).
ui_notes: Show influential citations separately from total citations.
note: Biases: full-text access skews by publisher and field; h-index ignores career stage and field norms (Semantic Scholar's own warning).

name: OpenAlex author summary_stats (h-index, i10, cited_by_count)
what: Author records with cited_by_count, works_count and summary_stats (h-index, i10-index); the authors endpoint can sort by them.
why_it_matters: Free, open, and joinable to people by ORCID; the scholar-side works signal for our people graph.
numbers: Fields: cited_by_count, works_count, summary_stats.h_index, summary_stats.i10_index (OpenAlex author object docs). OpenAlex vs Scopus rank correlation is high in an arXiv study (arXiv 2404.17663), but author disambiguation was not checked.
ui_notes: Show h-index with works count and field; do not rank across fields on h-index alone.
note: Biases: field and career-length; author disambiguation errors; no method page for the author ranking itself was found.

name: Measuring academic influence: Not all citations are equal (arXiv 1501.06587)
what: Argues the h-index treats a highly cited and barely cited paper alike once they clear the threshold, and proposes weighting citations by influence, tested on ACL Fellows.
why_it_matters: Justifies weighting citations rather than counting them, the same logic as the Semantic Scholar influential flag.
numbers: Tested on ACL Fellows (search summary; check paper for correlation numbers).
ui_notes: If we show a works score, state that it is a weighted citation score, not an h-index.
note: Bias: field-dependent citation norms; h-index cannot compare across fields.

name: TIME 100 Most Influential People
what: Annual editor-curated list; nominations from alumni and international writing staff; separate Reader's Poll picks one winner.
why_it_matters: A human editorial gold-standard style list we can use as a validation set (who is on it, and in what year), not as a score.
numbers: No score; editors choose; Time's 2026 statement says there is no single metric for influence (KUTV coverage, https://kutv.com/news/entertainment/times-100-most-influential-people-of-2026-who-made-the-cut-noah-wyle-hilary-duff-alysa-liu-rhea-seehorn-victoria-beckham-hilary-knight-nikki-glaser).
ui_notes: Show as a badge (on Time 100 in year X) rather than a rank.
note: Biases: editor and alumni networks, US and media-facing people; no transparent method beyond the nomination process.

name: Forbes Celebrity 100 (earnings plus fame)
what: Ranks celebrities by earnings over a 12-month window plus a fame score built from Google hits, Blog Search, LexisNexis TV and radio mentions, Factiva press, magazine covers and social followers; a 2013 marketability score from E-Poll was added.
why_it_matters: The clearest mixed-signal commercial method: separates earnings from fame, and is a template for a fame-by-channel breakdown.
numbers: Earnings window June 2009 to June 2010 (2010 edition, Globe and Mail); fame counts 25 consumer magazines; 2013 marketability score 1-100 across 6,600 celebrities polled on 46 attributes (goodblacknews.org 2013).
ui_notes: Show the fame breakdown by channel, not one number; show a year stamp because the method has changed.
note: Biases: US-centric media sources (LexisNexis, US magazines), earnings favor film/TV, editorial opacity on the fame score. Forbes India 2026 article found in search is unreliable (illustrative table).

name: Klout (dead social influence score)
what: Social influence score 0-100 from cumulative online actions; bought by Lithium in 2014 and shut down on May 25, 2018.
why_it_matters: Evidence that a black-box influence score on platform activity does not survive; its failure is about opacity and platform dependence, not just algorithm quality.
numbers: Shut down 2018-05-25; Lithium reportedly paid about $200M in 2014 (Search Engine Journal and coverage; price is a secondary-source figure).
ui_notes: If we publish a score, publish the formula and the inputs; Klout's black-box score was the core complaint.
note: Reasons: parent said standalone service not aligned with long-term strategy; critics said the score method was never clear. Caution against platform-dependent inputs (Twitter/Facebook).

name: Kred Influence and Outreach scores
what: Social influence score on a 1-1000 scale with separate Influence (others acting on your content) and Outreach (your activity) measures; founder-written description.
why_it_matters: A two-number design (influence received vs. activity given) that is worth copying for people ranking; the shutdown is NOT verified by our search.
numbers: Influence scale 1-1000 (founder post, 2012). Shutdown date not confirmed from our search.
ui_notes: Two-score layout: influence received and outreach given, shown side by side.
note: Status unknown; treat as defunct only after a primary source. Founder source, so promotional.

name: Famous Birthdays popularity ranking
what: Celebrity directory whose popularity list is driven by user boosts and likes, with a separate Trending list for recent boost spikes.
why_it_matters: A crowd-vote popularity signal; shows what a user-activity rank looks like at scale.
numbers: About 3 million uniques and 11 million page views a month in 2014 (OMR/SoCal Tech coverage; traffic, not ranking input).
ui_notes: Show Trending and All-time as two different tabs; label the signal as votes.
note: Biases: fan-base mobilization, young and US-skewed user base, vote manipulation; ranking not validated.

name: gitstar-ranking (k0kubun)
what: Open-source (MIT) self-hosted app that ranks GitHub users, organizations and repositories via the GitHub API.
why_it_matters: Reference implementation for a developer-side rank we can rebuild from GitHub API data; the people-graph has repo owners to feed it.
numbers: About 811 stars and 85 forks at capture (gittrend listing).
ui_notes: Show rank as a position with followers and stars as the displayed inputs.
note: Biases: GitHub-only; follower counts reward self-promotion; the ranking formula was not read in this slice (check the repo README).

name: Star History top-committer rank (GitHub commits)
what: Badge that ranks GitHub users among the top committers to the 20,000 most-starred repos and among the 20,000 most-followed users, based on public commit-contribution counts.
why_it_matters: A contribution-count rank that is an alternative to star or follower-based scores; directly usable for repo owners in our graph.
numbers: Universe: 20,000 most-followed users; 20,000 most-starred repos (Star History pages dated 2026-09-14).
ui_notes: Show the badge only when in the universe; say the universe in the caption.
note: Biases: commit counts reward bots and big-org monorepo contributors; universe is capped at the most-followed and most-starred.

name: Top contributors to GitHub 2017 (Felipe Hoffa)
what: Ranking of top GitHub contributors by PushEvent counts grouped by organization, limited to repos with at least 20 stars that year.
why_it_matters: A worked example of building a contributor rank from GH Archive events; reproducible with our own data pipeline.
numbers: Threshold: repos with at least 20 stars in the year (article). Counts per user from PushEvents.
ui_notes: Show a per-org grouping so a single company does not dominate.
note: Biases: push count rewards bots and automation; org grouping hides individuals; 2017 data, old.

name: OSS Insight (PingCAP) repository rankings
what: Real-time repository collection rankings from 10 billion GitHub events, ranking repos by stars, PRs, issues and PR creators over the last 28 days, with yearly history back to 2011.
why_it_matters: Event-based rolling-window ranking pattern to copy for works (repos) and for people (PR creators).
numbers: 10 billion GitHub events; 28-day window; history since 2011 (collection pages). No developer-ranking formula found in search.
ui_notes: Show three metrics as tabs over a 28-day window and a yearly view.
note: Biases: recent-window bias; collections chosen by the site; no developer formula checked.

name: Round-robin pairwise LLM judging with Bradley-Terry (arXiv 2502.14074)
what: Shows round-robin pairwise judging plus Bradley-Terry reduces non-transitivity and gives rankings that match Chatbot Arena human rankings better than fixed baselines.
why_it_matters: The method to rank people or works by LLM judgement without an O(N) baseline bias; applicable to a head-to-head judge of notable people.
numbers: Position switching cuts non-transitivity effects by 17% to 44% for stronger judges (paper summary in search).
ui_notes: Show the rank as a Bradley-Terry score with a 95% interval, not a point.
note: Biases: judge model's own knowledge and training data (Western, English and recent); position bias; verbosity and self-preference bias. Cost O(N squared) pairs, so use sampling.

name: Judging the Judges: systematic study of position bias in pairwise LLM-as-a-judge (arXiv 2406.07791)
what: Systematic study of position bias across many LLM judges and candidate pairs; finds bias is systematic and depends on quality gap between candidates.
why_it_matters: Required reading before any LLM-as-judge people ranking: the bias is not random noise and does not vanish with prompt length changes.
numbers: Across about 12 to 15 judges and about 40 candidate models (summary in search; verify exact numbers in paper).
ui_notes: Show a position-consistency rate next to any LLM-judged rank.
note: Bias: position bias; quality-gap dependence means close pairs flip more.

name: TrueSkill and Elo for pairwise ranking (no people-notability use found)
what: Rating systems that treat each item as a distribution (TrueSkill: mean plus variance) and update on pairwise outcomes; TrueSkill supports multi-player and new items without recomputing others.
why_it_matters: A way to turn human pairwise judgments of people into a rank with uncertainty; no notability study using it was found.
numbers: TrueSkill: mean and variance per player (Wikipedia). GitRanking (arXiv 2205.09379) uses it for GitHub topics with active sampling.
ui_notes: Show a rank plus an uncertainty band that narrows as votes accumulate.
note: Biases: rater pool (who votes), familiarity bias (people vote for names they know), and Elo misspecification under model error (arXiv 2502.10985).

name: NameRank: measuring recognition of people and entities in LLMs (arXiv 2607.12520)
what: Probes 4,685 entities across 36 models with one question each; an independent judge scores whether the model states a specific, checkable fact; yields a [0,1] recognition score.
why_it_matters: A model-side fame measure that can be cross-checked against Wikipedia and pageview ranks, and shows bibliometrics explain little of recognition.
numbers: 4,685 entities, 54 cohorts, 36 models; citations explain about a third of recognition; Nobel, Turing, Fields laureates saturate (abstract, Jul 2026).
ui_notes: Use as a second axis: model recognition vs. our composite.
note: Biases: LLM training-data bias (English, Western, recent); gender inference in the paper relies on Western-name dictionaries and drops many East Asian names.
